sentences.text: Staurikosaurus was a small, agile, bipedal predator that measured between 2.2 and 2.25 meters in length, stood 80 centimeters tall, and weighed 30 kilograms.
This species was considerably smaller than its relative Herrerasaurus, possessing a femur length of 23 centimeters compared to 47 centimeters.
The first known specimen, catalogued as MCZ 1669, was found by paleontologist Llewellyn Ivor Price in 1936 at the Jazigo Cinco site in the Santa Maria Formation, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil.
The genus was named by Edwin Harris Colbert in 1970.
The available teeth suggest a carnivorous diet, as the animal hunted small to medium-sized terrestrial vertebrates including cynodonts, rhynchosaurs, and herbivorous synapsids.
These teeth were serrated, laterally compressed, and curved backward toward the throat, likely helping to process smaller prey by working it backwards toward the throat.
The mandible suggests it had a sliding joint allowing the jaw to move backwards, forwards, up, and down.
The tail was relatively long, containing more than 40 vertebrae.
Ostrom suggested that this stiffened tail served as a dynamic stabilizer for leaping and running.
Staurikosaurus is classified within the clade Herrerasauridae according to the scientific consensus established since 1994.
Colbert originally misclassified Staurikosaurus in the defunct family Palaeosauriscidae before it was moved to Herrerasauridae.
Staurikosaurus lived approximately 225 million years ago during the late-Carnian and early-Norian stages of the Late Triassic in what is now South America.
The environment where it lived was arid to semi-arid, featuring seed ferns, ferns, cycads, and conifers.
Garcia et al. (2019) referred the holotype of Teyuwasu barberenai as a second specimen of Staurikosaurus pricei, a proposal that remains controversial.
